query: We are investigating the anomalous ductile-brittle-ductile transition in an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA aged in the 550-750°C regime. The baseline as-cast material is ductile. Aging at ~600°C induces a brittle state characterized by a loss of elongation, while aging at ~750°C restores ductility. The failure mechanism is hypothesized to stem from the coupled evolution of L12 ordered domains and jagged phase boundaries, distinct from conventional temper embrittlement. Specifically, the hypothesis is that excessive ordering (near stoichiometric Ni3Al ratios) within the FCC matrix, combined with jagged B2/FCC interfaces, creates a high antiphase boundary energy (APBE) and restricts cross-slip, leading to planar slip and stress concentration at boundary serrations. Conversely, higher aging temperatures reduce the order degree and form ductile transition zones along the PBs. Formulate a hypothesis detailing the specific atomic-scale mechanism (e.g., APBE changes, SISFE modulation) driving the brittle window. What is the critical boundary for the transition in terms of chemical ordering? Propose a falsification experiment using nanoindentation or transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to distinguish this mechanism from simple phase decomposition, and predict the specific structural feature (e.g., jagged PBs) that must be observed to confirm the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The brittle window in aged AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA (550–750°C) is driven by a critical threshold of L12 ordering degree that maximizes Antiphase Boundary Energy (APBE) and minimizes Stacking Fault Energy (SISFE) in the FCC matrix, causing planar slip and stress localization at jagged B2/FCC interfaces; this brittleness is reversed at higher temperatures (>750°C) where thermal energy reduces the L12 order parameter, lowering APBE and restoring cross-slip capability.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with a ductile dual-phase microstructure (FCC matrix + B2 precipitates) and smooth phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Isothermal aging at 600°C for a duration sufficient to induce peak L12 ordering (near-stoichiometric Ni3Al ratios) versus aging at 750°C to induce partial disordering.
generation.conditions: Aging temperatures between 550°C and 750°C in an inert atmosphere; mechanical testing at room temperature to assess ductility loss.
generation.structural_mediator: Jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries and the degree of L12 long-range order (LRO) within the FCC matrix precipitates.
generation.mechanism: At ~600°C, the formation of highly ordered L12 domains increases the APBE, which restricts the dissociation width of Shockley partials and inhibits cross-slip. This forces dislocations to move via planar slip, concentrating stress at the geometric irregularities (serrations) of the jagged B2/FCC interfaces, leading to premature crack nucleation. At ~750°C, the LRO parameter decreases, reducing APBE and allowing dislocations to cross-slip, thereby blunting stress concentrations and restoring ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: A non-monotonic ductility curve where elongation drops to a minimum at ~600°C (high APBE, jagged PBs) and recovers at ~750°C (lower APBE, smoother or transition-zone PBs). TEM analysis will show a direct correlation between the peak in L12 order parameter and the maximum APBE/SISFE ratio.
generation.baseline: Conventional temper embrittlement mechanisms driven solely by solute segregation to grain boundaries without significant changes in matrix ordering or APBE.
generation.boundary: The transition is bounded by the critical L12 order parameter (η) where APBE exceeds the critical stress required for cross-slip; below this threshold (higher T), ductility is restored.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical value of the L12 order parameter (η) required to trigger the brittle transition is unknown without direct measurement of APBE in this specific alloy system. The specific contribution of 'jagged' boundary morphology versus pure ordering effects cannot be fully decoupled without high-resolution in-situ TEM.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in-situ nanoindentation on aged samples (600°C vs 750°C) combined with high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) and Selected Area Electron Diffraction (SAED) to map local dislocation activity and order parameters simultaneously. Specifically, indent near B2/FCC interfaces to observe slip transmission.
measurements: Local Stacking Fault Energy (SISFE) derived from dislocation dissociation width in HRTEM.
Antiphase Boundary Energy (APBE) estimated from the critical stress for cross-slip in the L12 precipitates.
Order parameter (η) quantification via SAED superlattice spot intensity.
Dislocation character (screw vs edge) and slip planarity (planar vs wavy) via TEM diffraction contrast analysis.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hypothesis is false, samples aged at 600°C (brittle) will NOT show a significantly higher L12 order parameter or APBE compared to 750°C samples, OR dislocations will exhibit wavy slip (cross-slip) even in the brittle state despite high ordering, indicating that ordering is not the primary driver of the ductile-brittle transition.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a lot of attention in recent years, due to the unique combinations of structural, physical and chemical properties of these alloys [1] – [3] . HEAs usually form simple structures such as body-centered cubic (BCC) (e.g. TaNbHfZrTi [4] , NbTaVWZr [5] etc.) or face-centered cubic (FCC) (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi [6] , CoCrFeMnNi [7] etc.) solid solutions. The large number of the alloying elements in near-equiatomic proportions result in high configurational entropy in these solid solutions. However, these alloys can decompose to multiple phases upon changing the composition or annealing at different temperatures or a combination of both [8] – [10] . Such a phase decomposition is often the result of the complex interplay of configurational entropy of mixing with the enthalpies of mixing of the constituent elements. Additionally, such multiphase microstructures are more likely to exhibit the desired properties for real engineering applications. Hence, tuning the composition and fractions of phases is critical for achieving the desired properties [10] , [11] .

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), as a novel type of material generally consisting of five or more principle elements, have attracted extensive attention in recent years because of their attractive crystallographic and mechanical properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Although it is anticipated that simple solid solution phases are easier to form rather than the intermetallic compounds or complex-ordered phases due to their high configurational entropy [ [8] , [9] ], only a few HEAs have exactly single and stable solid solution structures, among which CoCrFeNiMn alloy is widely concerned [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. It possesses a single face-center-cubic (fcc) solid solution phase even after a series of thermomechanical processing [ [15] , [16] ] and its constituent elements have more sluggish diffusion compared to other conventional alloys [ [17] ]. These characterizations contribute to excellent mechanical properties with a satisfactory combination between tensile strength and ductility [ [18] , [19] ].
